summary: This memo specifies the Identification Protocol, formerly called the Authentication Server Protocol, which lets a server ask a remote host which user owns a particular TCP connection. It was renamed to better reflect its function. The answer is only as trustworthy as the host giving it.

plainLanguage.summary: Ident is a small service on a host that answers one question: who owns this particular TCP connection? You connect to port 113, send the two port numbers of the connection you mean, and the host replies with a name such as a login, or with an error explaining why it will not say. The document is emphatic that the answer is worth exactly as much as the honesty of the host giving it.

questions: how to identify the user of a tcp connection
how does ident find the owner of a tcp connection
is the ident protocol safe for access control
subtitle: A small TCP service that names the user behind a connection, and why its answer is only as good as the host that gives it.

tldr.problem: An administrator looking at a connection often wants to know which user it belongs to, and there was no standard way to ask the machine that owns the connection.
tldr.mechanism: A server listens on TCP port 113. The client opens a connection, sends the port pair of the connection it is asking about, and the server replies with either the user identifier of that connection or an error explaining why it could not say.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the query and reply formats, the two response types, the permitted error codes and the length limits. It was formerly called the Authentication Server Protocol and was renamed, and it states plainly that the answer is only as trustworthy as the host that gives it and must not be used for access control.

today: RFC 1413 is a Proposed Standard from February 1993 and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 931, the Authentication Server Protocol, and renamed the protocol to match what it actually does. The document itself states that the answer is only as trustworthy as the host providing it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Identification Protocol, also known as ident or the Ident Protocol, provides a means to determine the identity of a user of a particular TCP connection. Given a TCP port number pair, it returns a character string that identifies the owner of that connection on the server's system.

The protocol was formerly called the Authentication Server Protocol. It was renamed to better reflect its function, and the document is a product of the IETF TCP Client Identity Protocol Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: Ident answers a question about a connection: whose connection is it? You give it the two port numbers and it gives you a name. It used to be called the Authentication Server Protocol, but it does not authenticate anything, so the name was changed.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
This is a connection-based application on TCP. A server listens for TCP connections on TCP port 113. Once a connection is established, the server reads a line of data that specifies the connection of interest. If that connection exists, the system-dependent user identifier of the connection of interest is sent as the reply. The server may then either shut the connection down or continue to read and answer multiple queries.

The server should close the connection after a configurable amount of time with no queries, and a 60 to 180 second idle timeout is recommended. The client may close the connection at any time, but to allow for network delays the client should wait at least 30 seconds, or longer, after a query before abandoning the query and closing the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The service is a listener on port 113 that reads one line per question. The client asks, gets an answer, and waits half a minute before giving up on a question that has not been answered. The server drops the connection after a minute or two of silence, or after three minutes at the far end of the recommended range.

sections.title: Restrictions
sections.content: Queries are permitted only for fully specified connections. The query contains the local and foreign port pair, and the local and foreign address pair used to fully specify the connection is taken from the local and foreign addresses of the query connection itself. In other words, a user on address A may only ask the server on address B about connections between A and B.
sections.plainLanguage: The server only answers about connections that involve the machine asking the question. You cannot use ident on one host to look up a connection that has nothing to do with that host, because the server uses the addresses of the query connection itself to decide which connection you mean.

sections.title: Query and Response Format
sections.content:
The server accepts simple text query requests of the form port-on-server, port-on-client, where the first number is the TCP port in decimal on the target system, where the ident server is running, and the second is the TCP port in decimal on the source system.

The order of the two ports is the reverse of what the client sees locally. If a client on host A wants to ask a server on host B about a connection that is specified locally on the client's machine as 23, 6191, an inbound TELNET connection, the client must actually ask about 6191, 23, which is how the connection is specified on host B. The document's example query is therefore 6191, 23.

The response has the form port-on-server, port-on-client, then a response type, then additional information: the two ports are the same pair as in the query, the response type is a keyword identifying the type of response, and the additional information depends on the type. The information returned is that associated with the fully specified TCP connection identified by the server address, the client address, the port on the server and the port on the client, where the two addresses are the local and foreign IP addresses of the querying connection, that is, of the connection to the ident server itself. The examples given are 6193, 23 : USERID : UNIX : stjohns and 6195, 23 : ERROR : NO-USER.

The formal syntax is short. A request is a port pair followed by the end of line, a reply is reply text followed by the end of line, and the end of line is the two octets 015 012, a carriage return and a line feed. A reply is either an error reply or an ident reply, and the ident reply is a port pair, the keyword USERID, an operating system field and the user identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The query is two port numbers and a line break. The order matters: the port on the machine that owns the connection comes first, even though the client sees the other end first. The reply repeats those two numbers, then says either USERID or ERROR, then gives the detail.

sections.title: Response Types and Syntax Rules
sections.content:
A response is one of two types. With USERID, the additional information is an operating system name, with an optional character set identifier, followed by a colon and the identification string. The character set, if present, is separated from the operating system name by a comma, and it defaults to US-ASCII when omitted. The permitted operating system names and character set names are specified in the Assigned Numbers document. There is one special case, OTHER. Unless OTHER is specified, the server is expected to return the normal user identification of the owner of the connection: a string that uniquely identifies the connection owner, such as a user identifier assigned by the system administrator and used by that user as a mail identifier, or the user part of a user and password pair used to gain access to system resources. When an operating system is specified, the identifier is expected to be in a form that is more or less immediately useful, for example something that could be used as an argument to finger or as a mail address. OTHER means the identifier is an unformatted string of printable characters in the specified character set, and it should be used when the user identifier does not meet those constraints, for example when sending an encrypted audit token or when returning other non-userid information about a user, such as the real name and phone number from a UNIX passwd file.

The identifier itself is an unformatted octet string: all octets are permissible except octal 000, 012 and 015, that is NUL, line feed and carriage return. Space characters after the colon separator are part of the identifier string and may not be ignored. The reply is still terminated normally by a carriage return and line feed, and those two are not part of the identifier. A string may be printable but is not necessarily printable.

With ERROR, the port owner could not be determined and the additional information says why. INVALID-PORT means the local or foreign port was improperly specified, which should be returned if either or both port identifiers were out of range, since TCP port numbers run from 1 to 65535, or were negative integers, reals, or otherwise not recognised as a non-negative integer. NO-USER means the connection specified by the port pair is not currently in use, or is not owned by an identifiable entity. HIDDEN-USER means the server was able to identify the user but the information was not returned at the request of the user. UNKNOWN-ERROR means the connection owner cannot be determined and the reason is unknown; any error not covered above should return this value. A server may return it in place of any other specific code, for example to hide information, but if it does that the feature MUST be configurable and it MUST default to returning the proper error message. A non-standard error code must begin with X. The server is also allowed to drop the query connection without responding, and any premature close is to be considered the same as an ERROR with an UNKNOWN-ERROR status.

The notes on syntax add the practical details. The syntax embodies the philosophy of being conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept: clients and servers should not generate unnecessary white space but should accept white space anywhere except within a token, and any amount of white space is permitted at the beginning or end of a line, for queries and responses alike. That does not apply to a user identifier, because everything after the colon following the operating system type up to the terminating carriage return and line feed is taken as part of the identifier. A client should feel free to abort a connection if it receives 1000 characters without an end of line. The limits mean that no new token, whether an operating system or an error type, will be longer than 64 characters, a server SHOULD NOT send more than 512 octets of user identifier, and a client MUST accept at least 512 octets, so a server MUST return the most significant part of the identifier in the first 512 octets. Character set identifiers apply only to the user identification field; all other fields are defined in and must be sent as US-ASCII. A client that does not recognise the returned character set should handle the string as octets but should still store or report the character set, and an octet string should be printed, stored or handled in hex notation as well as in any other representation the client implements.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of answer. USERID names the operating system and then the user, and the user identifier may contain any character except NUL, line feed and carriage return, so it can hold spaces and odd bytes. ERROR says why there is no name, and the codes cover the usual reasons: a port number that makes no sense, a connection that is not there, a user who asked not to be named, and a catch-all. The length limits keep the answer short: 512 octets for the name, 64 characters for a keyword.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The information returned by this protocol is at most as trustworthy as the host providing it or the organisation operating the host. A PC in an open lab has few if any controls to stop a user from having the protocol return any identifier the user wants. If the host has been compromised, the information returned may be completely erroneous and misleading.

The Identification Protocol is not intended as an authorization or access control protocol. At best it provides some additional auditing information about TCP connections; at worst it can provide misleading, incorrect or maliciously incorrect information. The use of the information for anything other than auditing is strongly discouraged, and specifically, using it to make access control decisions, either as the primary method with no other checks or as an adjunct to other methods, may result in a weakening of normal host security.

An ident server may also reveal information about users, entities, objects or processes that would normally be considered private. The document compares the service to the CallerID services provided by some phone companies, and says that the same privacy considerations and arguments that apply to CallerID apply here: if you would not run a finger server for privacy reasons, you may not want to run this protocol either.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is only as trustworthy as the machine that gives it, and a user can often choose what it says. The document is blunt about the consequence: do not use ident to decide who gets access to what, because trusting a name that the far end simply made up weakens the security of the host. The information is for auditing, and running the service publishes details about the users of the machine.

items.title: Port
items.text: 113, the TCP port the server listens on.

items.title: Client wait
items.text: At least 30 seconds after a query before giving up.

items.title: User identifier limit
items.text: 512 octets, of which the first part is the significant one.

items.title: Token limit
items.text: 64 characters for an operating system or error name.

items.title: Port range
items.text: TCP port numbers run from 1 to 65535.
